one_liner: Low-overhead general-purpose C/C++ malloc that usually beats glibc malloc on speed while using about as little memory.
what_it_does: Micro is a general-purpose allocator aimed at minimal memory overhead and fragmentation rather than peak speed. It exposes a C API (micro_malloc/micro_free, micro_heap_create/clear/destroy) and a C++ API (micro::heap), and a micro_proxy library replaces the system malloc via LD_PRELOAD-style tricks on Linux and DLL injection on Windows. Independent heaps can be freed in one call and can carve pages from a preallocated buffer or a memory-mapped file.
how_it_is_fast: Medium allocations (under 512 KiB) use a two-level radix tree of free chunks sorted by size with fine-grained locking: a true best-fit with immediate coalescing, O(1) like TLSF but exact instead of approximate. Small allocations (under 656 bytes by default) use 16-byte-spaced segregated size classes in 4 KiB-aligned blocks whose header is found by address masking, and those blocks are themselves carved from the radix tree. Threads are bound round-robin to per-core arenas instead of using thread-local caches, which keeps memory low and makes thread creation cheap (the reason it does well on Larson).
when_to_use: Replacing glibc malloc (or the Windows Low-fragmentation Heap) system-wide or per-process where resident memory matters more than the last bit of throughput.
Many-threaded programs where glibc malloc scales negatively and per-thread caches in jemalloc/mimalloc would inflate RSS.
Workloads that create and destroy many short-lived threads (Larson-style servers).
Arena-style code that wants independent heaps freed in one call, or allocation out of a fixed buffer or a memory-mapped file.
Small-memory systems: memory level 0 targets machines with only a few MBs.
when_not_to_use: Raw allocation throughput is the goal: the README says it is usually slower than mimalloc, snmalloc, tbbmalloc and jemalloc, and the cross-thread plot shows snmalloc and jemalloc well ahead.
Security-sensitive or attacker-facing heaps: the README states it has no hardening against heap exploitation.
macOS and Android: replacement of the system allocator is untested there per the README.
Huge-page dependent workloads: huge pages are not supported yet.
Projects that need a well-tested, widely deployed allocator: single author, 33 stars, test suite described as incomplete.

integration.form: static lib, shared lib, or header-only (define MICRO_HEADER_ONLY); micro_proxy for malloc replacement
integration.platforms: Linux and most Unix systems, Windows; macOS/Android untested for replacement
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe: per-core arenas with fine-grained locking in the radix tree; MICRO_NO_LOCK build option removes locking for single-threaded systems
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — link micro_proxy (or use the mp LD_PRELOAD tool) to replace malloc/free process-wide; otherwise call the micro_* API explicitly

gotchas: Memory profile is a compile-time choice (MICRO_MEMORY_LEVEL 0-4, default 2); levels 3-4 trade memory for speed, and the radix tree has a static per-arena cost that grows with the level.
Arena depletion (MICRO_DEPLETE_ARENAS=1, default) lowers memory at the expense of parallelism; behavior is also tunable through many MICRO_* environment variables read at startup.

With the file page provider, setting MICRO_PAGE_FILE_PROVIDER to a fixed filename makes spawned child processes share the same file ('certain crash' per the README); use MICRO_PAGE_FILE_PROVIDER_DIR instead.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over v8malloc or FastAlloc when lower RSS than glibc matters more than throughput, and over Mesh when you want low overhead without page meshing; pick a TLSF allocator like XenoAtom.Allocators or rlsf instead for a single-threaded or embedded pool with deterministic timing.
verified_claims_summary: First-party plots (md/benchmarks.md) compare micro with glibc 2.17, jemalloc 5.3.0, mimalloc 1.8 and snmalloc 3.14, built with gcc 10.3.0 (flags not stated) on a Xeon Gold 5220R under CentOS 7: same-thread alloc/free of random sizes up to 500 or 5000 bytes for 1-10 threads, a cross-thread random-free test and Larson, plotting Mops/s against peak-RSS/requested-bytes. Micro is faster than glibc with similar overhead, slower than snmalloc and jemalloc, and has the lowest overhead cross-thread; no numbers are given in text. Harness note from benchs/alloc_dealloc_same_thread.cpp: every allocator runs in sequence in one process (micro first), and overhead is computed from getrusage peak RSS, which is a lifetime maximum. If the plots came from such runs, later allocators' overhead can never read lower than micro's peak. The cleanup call (micro_clear, malloc_trim, mi_heap_collect) is inside the timed region, and snmalloc gets no cleanup.
status_note: Stale since late 2024 (one closed issue, single author) but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and usable header-only, so it is easy to trial via the mp LD_PRELOAD tool before committing.
